title: Remove Duplicate Letters
question: Why can a larger character be removed from the stack only when it appears again later?
answer: Removing it improves lexicographic order, but it is safe only if another occurrence remains to include that distinct character in the final result.

title: Remove Duplicate Letters
question: What prevents a character from appearing twice in the result?
answer: The seen array/set skips any character already in the stack. When a character is popped, its seen flag is cleared so a later occurrence can be chosen instead.

title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths
question: How does a bitmask detect whether two words share a letter?
answer: Each letter sets one bit. If the bitwise AND of two masks is zero, no letter bit is set in both words, so their character sets are disjoint.

title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths
question: What is the benefit of storing masks before checking pairs?
answer: It avoids scanning characters repeatedly for every pair. Mask construction is linear in total input characters, and each pair check is a constant-time bit operation.

title: Bulb Switcher
question: Why do only perfect-square bulb positions remain on?
answer: A bulb is toggled once per positive divisor. Divisors usually pair as d and i/d, but a perfect square has one unpaired square-root divisor, giving an odd toggle count.

title: Bulb Switcher
question: Why is the answer floor(sqrt(n))?
answer: The bulbs that remain on are at positions 1², 2², 3², and so on up to n. There are exactly floor(sqrt(n)) such squares.

title: Coin Change
question: What does dp[x] mean in the bottom-up coin-change algorithm?
answer: dp[x] is the minimum number of coins needed to form amount x using the denominations processed by the recurrence. Each transition considers a coin as the final coin.

title: Coin Change
question: How does the algorithm detect an impossible amount?
answer: Unreachable states retain a sentinel value amount+1. If dp[amount] remains greater than amount, no valid coin combination was found and the method returns -1.

title: Power of Three
question: Why can divisibility by 3^19 test powers of three in 32-bit integers?
answer: 3^19 is the largest power of three within the positive signed 32-bit range. Its positive divisors that are powers of three are exactly the smaller powers of three.

title: Power of Three
question: Why must zero and negative values be rejected first?
answer: A power of three is positive. The divisibility test alone would not express that definition, so the implementation checks n>0 before testing the remainder.

title: Odd Even Linked List
question: Why save the head of the even chain before rewiring pointers?
answer: The even nodes are detached and relinked during traversal. Keeping evenHead preserves the start of that chain so it can be attached after the final odd node.

title: Odd Even Linked List
question: What does the loop condition even != null && even.next != null ensure?
answer: Both the current even node and its following odd-position node exist, so the algorithm can safely relink one odd node and one even node per iteration.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
question: Why is memoized DFS safe from cycles in this matrix problem?
answer: Every recursive move goes to a strictly larger value. Values therefore increase along recursion, making cycles impossible; memoization computes each cell's result once.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
question: What does memo[r][c] store?
answer: It stores the maximum number of cells in a strictly increasing path that starts at matrix cell (r,c), including that cell itself.

title: Verify Preorder Serialization of a Binary Tree
question: How does child-slot counting validate a preorder serialization?
answer: A tree starts with one root slot. Every token consumes one slot; a non-null node adds two child slots. A valid serialization never runs out early and finishes with zero slots.

title: Verify Preorder Serialization of a Binary Tree
question: Why is it invalid if slots becomes zero before the last token?
answer: The tokens already describe a complete tree, so any remaining token would have no parent slot to occupy. A valid serialization must end exactly when all slots are filled.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
question: Why are destinations consumed in lexical order but airports appended after recursion?
answer: Hierholzer traversal must use every ticket and may need to backtrack when a locally small choice leads to a dead end. Postorder appending and reversing produces the lexicographically smallest valid itinerary.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
question: Why is a priority queue useful for each airport?
answer: It exposes the lexicographically smallest remaining destination efficiently. Each ticket is removed exactly once as the DFS follows outgoing edges.

title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
question: Why does finding a value greater than both first and second prove a triplet exists?
answer: first is an earlier small candidate and second was assigned only after finding a value strictly greater than first. A later value above second completes the ordered triple.

title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
question: Why do the comparisons use <= when updating first and second?
answer: The triplet must be strictly increasing. Equal values cannot extend a valid pair, so they replace a tail candidate rather than triggering success.
